text:
alex: quick q — trying to script non-interactive token refresh for long-running infra cron jobs. currently we `redwood auth login --profile infra-ci` once and export env vars, but tokens expire after an hour. what patterns are people using for automated refresh without storing raw creds in files?

jen: we run a small systemd service that calls `redwood auth refresh` and writes to /run/redwood/creds.env, then our workers source that. keeps creds out of home dir and it rotates.

sam: fwiw we use the keyring backend on linux (libsecret) + a short daemon that calls the CLI and updates a file with only the ephemeral token, not the long-term client secret. keyring stores the refresh token encrypted.

maria: +1 to keyring if you can. if you need fully headless (CI) use a dedicated machine account with minimal perms and keep the long-term credential in your CI secrets manager, then run a tiny renovver container that exchanges and writes ephemeral creds to a shared volume.

alex: thanks. curious about precedence: when I run `redwood --profile infra-ci` vs REDWOOD_PROFILE env var vs `--api-key` directly, what's the order? I couldn't find it in the CLI help.

jen: precedence we use in our scripts: explicit flag > env var > profile file (~/.redwood/config) > system config (/etc/redwood/config). worth confirming in docs but that's what the code does now.

sam: confirmed in code recently: --api-key/--profile on cmdline wins, then REDWOOD_API_KEY / REDWOOD_PROFILE, then user config, then system. also `REDWOOD_CLI_CACHE` can change where ephemeral tokens are stored.

ci-bot: reminder: for infra-ci profile we've set session TTL=1h and refresh-token TTL=7d. rotate the long-lived secret monthly.

alex: any safe bash snippet folks recommend? I want something simple to run as a cron every 45m and atomically swap the env file.

jen: this is what we do (pseudo):
```
#!/bin/bash
TMP=$(mktemp)
redwood auth refresh --profile infra-ci --non-interactive --format env > "$TMP"
chmod 600 "$TMP"
mv "$TMP" /run/redwood/creds.env
# optional: systemctl kill -s HUP my-worker to pick up new env
```

maria: make sure `auth refresh` exits non-zero on failure so cron can alert, and don't echo secrets in logs. use `--format env` so it's ready to `source`.

alex: ok. one more: Python async streaming quirk — when worker reloads env, background event loop still has old token and streaming requests start failing with 401 mid-stream. anyone handled hot-reload without restarting workers?

sam: we solved by using a token provider callback in the client. instead of caching token at import time, client calls a small function that reads /run/redwood/creds.env before each request (or on auth failure tries refresh once). avoids restart.

maria: pattern: wrap transport with a short-circuit that on 401 will call the refresher once and retry the request. that covers in-flight mid-stream 401s. downside: adds one extra retry latency.

alex: solid, thanks. last Q: Windows devs — any tips for scripting renewals there?

jen: use wincred or credential manager + a scheduled task that runs `redwood.exe auth refresh --profile infra-ci --format env > C:\\run\\redwood\\creds.env`. scheduled task can run as service account.

alex: awesome, very helpful. I'll prototype the systemd/refresher + provider-callback pattern and post back with snippets. :thumbsup:
